analysis.one_liner: Limits lawsuits and damages over Year 2000 computer failures.
analysis.headline: Thirteen senators — nine Republicans and four Democrats — cosponsored this Y2K lawsuit-limiting bill, which never got a vote, but a nearly identical Y2K liability law passed anyway and was signed in July 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules for lawsuits over Year 2000 computer failures: capping punitive damages, making each defendant pay only its own share of fault, requiring a 30-day written notice plus a fix-it window before anyone could sue, strictly enforcing contract clauses that limit liability, and barring most claims for lost profits and business downtime. It excluded personal injury and wrongful death claims. It never received a vote, but Congress passed a nearly identical bill that became law instead.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies facing Y2K lawsuits — software and computer makers, banks, insurers, utilities, and any business whose products or systems failed on January 1, 2000. Punitive damages would be capped (at the lesser of three times compensatory damages or $250,000 for individuals worth under $500,000 and firms with fewer than 50 employees, and only on clear and convincing evidence); each defendant would pay only its percentage of fault except in cases of intentional injury or knowing fraud; a plaintiff would have to send detailed written notice and wait 30 days — plus 60 more if the defendant proposes a fix — before filing; contract clauses capping or disclaiming liability would be strictly enforced; and claims for economic loss like lost profits and business interruption would be barred in tort unless a contract or direct physical damage supported them. Small defendants got extra protection, and personal injury and wrongful death claims stayed outside the bill's limits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Software, tech, and financial firms facing lawsuits

how_it_helps.text: Caps punitive damages in Y2K suits at the lesser of three times compensatory damages or $250,000 for individuals with a net worth under $500,000 and businesses with fewer than 50 employees, and requires plaintiffs to prove their case by clear and convincing evidence.

Replaces joint and several liability with proportionate liability — each defendant pays only its share of fault — keeping defendants fully on the hook only if they intended injury or knowingly committed fraud.

Forces a would-be plaintiff to send detailed written notice of the defect and the harm, then wait 30 days for a response and up to 60 more for a proposed fix before filing suit, pushing disputes toward repair and mediation instead of court.

Strictly enforces written contract terms — including liability limits and warranty disclaimers — and bars tort recovery of economic loss such as lost profits, business interruption, and consequential damages unless a contract or direct damage to property supports it.
Keeps claims for personal injury and wrongful death entirely outside the bill's limits, so people physically harmed by a Y2K failure would keep normal remedies.

Restricts class actions to defects material to a majority of the class, requires detailed notice and fee disclosure to class members, and moves large Y2K class actions (over $1 million) into federal court.

analysis.who_pays: The businesses and consumers who bought technology that failed. When a system crashed on January 1, 2000, the buyer — not the seller — would absorb most of the loss: lost profits, business downtime, and most consequential damages become unrecoverable unless a contract says otherwise. Even a winning plaintiff could be left short, because each defendant pays only its share of fault and, for most plaintiffs, extra liability for a co-defendant's uncollectible share is capped at 50 percent of each defendant's share. The bill would also override state laws that give plaintiffs stronger remedies, and plaintiffs' lawyers would lose the fee-generating suits the bill is designed to shrink.
analysis.who_pays_short: Customers of failed tech, and trial lawyers

drawbacks.text: The bill shifts the cost of defective or non-compliant technology from the companies that sold it to the businesses and people who bought it: lost profits, business interruption, and consequential damages are unrecoverable in tort unless a contract or direct property damage supports them.

Even plaintiffs who win can go unpaid: each defendant pays only its percentage of fault, and except for small individuals (net worth under $200,000 whose damages exceed 10 percent of that net worth), other defendants' responsibility for an uncollectible share is capped at 50 percent of their own share.
The pre-litigation notice and remediation rules can add up to 90 days before a lawsuit may even be filed, delaying money for a small firm trying to recover from a crash.
The act preempts inconsistent state law, wiping out stronger state consumer and contract protections for Y2K disputes, and raises the bar for class actions that aggregate many small claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real worry: a wave of Y2K litigation could have pulled engineers and executives into courtrooms instead of fixing code, and its defenders could point to the carve-out for personal injury and the preservation of suits for real, contract-backed losses. But its main effect is to move the cost of failed technology from sellers to buyers. The parties with the most at stake were the large technology and financial firms with the greatest lawsuit exposure, and the narrow punitive-damage caps and fault-sharing rules do little for a small customer left holding a dead system. The bill was tilted toward concentrated interests, with modest safeguards for small defendants and small plaintiffs on the way.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but it was never brought to a vote — the Senate instead passed a nearly identical Y2K liability bill that became law.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain introduced the bill on May 26, 1999 with 13 cosponsors from both parties, and it was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 125) the next day.
No committee acted on it and no vote was ever scheduled; the record ends with the bill sitting on the calendar, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with it never having come to the floor.

The substance did not die: the Senate passed a nearly identical Y2K liability bill (S. 96) in June 1999, and a version was signed into law by President Clinton that July, so the lawsuit limits this bill proposed became law under a different number.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies facing Y2K lawsuits — software, technology, and financial firms above all — came out ahead: the liability protections this bill embodied were enacted anyway under a different bill number, while opponents of those limits got nothing.

for.name: John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-AZ), bill sponsor and Commerce Committee chairman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar within a day.

for.name: 13 Senate cosponsors (9 Republicans, 4 Democrats)
for.role: Cosponsors including Dodd, Lieberman, Wyden, Feinstein, Hatch, Bennett, and Lott
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support from both parties' leadership ranks.

against.name: Consumer and civil-justice groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed capping damages and limiting fault-based liability for Y2K failures, arguing the rules would stick customers with the cost of defective products.

against.name: 18 senators, nearly all Democrats
against.role: No votes on final passage of the companion Y2K bill (S. 96)
against.what_they_did: Voted against the Senate's near-identical Y2K liability bill on the floor in June 1999.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 9 of the 13 cosponsors were Republicans and 4 were Democrats, including senior figures from both parties — and the near-identical law that eventually passed cleared the Senate by a wide bipartisan vote.

industries.note: The bill caps their punitive damages, limits them to paying only their share of fault, requires a notice-and-fix window before suit, and enforces their liability disclaimers — so when their products failed on January 1, 2000, their customers bore most of the loss. This was the bill's core constituency.

Y2K failures in payment systems, mortgages, and credit reporting threatened a flood of claims; the bill bars most economic-loss suits and caps damages, leaving customers to absorb errors in their accounts. Banks and financial firms were among the most exposed defendants.

Fewer, smaller Y2K claims mean fewer payouts on liability and errors-and-omissions policies. The same firms sold Y2K coverage, so limiting what policyholders could recover from third parties cut the insurers' exposure from both directions.

Service failures from embedded-chip problems would generate far less damages liability, since customers could not recover lost profits or business interruption absent a contract or direct property damage.

The bill is built to shrink Y2K litigation — notice requirements, pleading hurdles, damage caps, and class-action limits all reduce the volume and value of suits on which plaintiffs' attorneys work. Their loss tracks the loss of the customers they would have represented.
